query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid computational framework that explicitly decouples lattice and electronic heat transport contributions in HfNbTaTiZr by incorporating realistic atomistic disorder and defect effects will predict temperature‐dependent thermal conductivity with an accuracy of ±10%, compared to the ±30% error of previous perfect-crystal based models.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr alloy modeled as both near-perfect, defect-free crystals (for low temperature studies) and as defect-rich systems (including ~1 wt.% oxygen) at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Apply a hybrid DFT-plus-transport method (integrating Green–Kubo and Boltzmann transport approaches) that incorporates atomic-scale disorder and explicit defect distributions to separately compute lattice and electronic contributions.
generation.conditions: Predictions are made for two regimes: low temperature (<200 K) where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable, and high temperature (300–1200 K) including conditions with ~1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale disorder and defect structures (including oxygen impurities) that modify vibrational and electronic transport channels.
generation.mechanism: By integrating first-principles DFT calculations with transport methodologies (Green-Kubo/Boltzmann), the framework explicitly accounts for the non-ideal atomic environments and defect-induced scattering. This decoupling allows separate computation of lattice and electronic heat transport, overcoming the limitations of previous analytical approaches that assumed defect-free crystals.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method will yield thermal conductivity predictions with overall errors reduced to approximately ±10% relative to experiments, accurately reproducing the distinct contributions at low (<200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperatures.
generation.baseline: Traditional analytical and simulation approaches that use perfect, defect-free bulk crystal assumptions, which have exhibited prediction errors of around ±30%.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies specifically to the HfNbTaTiZr alloy and similar refractory high-entropy alloys within the temperature range from below 200 K (where electronic and lattice contributions are comparable) to 1200 K (including samples with intentional oxygen contamination). Extrapolation beyond these conditions or to alloys with significantly different defect chemistries remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While preliminary evidence supports an expected improvement in predictive accuracy, uncertainties in the exact scaling of defect effects and sample-to-sample variations may influence the accuracy margin. Further experimental validation is needed to conclusively confirm the ±10% error target.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled defect densities, including near-perfect samples and samples with ~1 wt.% oxygen. Measure the total thermal conductivity and separately resolve the lattice and electronic contributions over two temperature ranges (below 200 K and between 300–1200 K). Compare the experimental data with the predictions of the hybrid model.
measurements: Total thermal conductivity as a function of temperature
Separated lattice and electronic thermal conductivity (using techniques such as differential measurements and spectroscopic methods)
Characterization of defect densities and impurity levels (e.g., via TEM, XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hybrid model’s predictions deviate by more than ±10% from the experimentally measured thermal conductivities across both temperature regimes, or if it fails to clearly decouple the lattice and electronic contributions relative to traditional models (which show errors around ±30%), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
